speechtext:

That the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, responsible for licences on import quotas, suspend for a three-month period all import licences on those products to undertake a complete review of any import policy to stabilize the Canadian production for threatened producers.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ENFORCEMENT OF REGULATIONS CONCERNING LICENSING OF AIR CREW-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. My motion is prompted by the fact that as of Friday, April 9, approximately 3,500 pilots whose licences have expired are breaking the law, in particular the Aeronautics Act. Air regulations section 400 states that, except as provided in this part, no person shall fly or attempt to fly as a flight crew member of an aircraft unless he is the holder of a valid and subsisting licence or permit appropriate to his duties issued under this part.
Because this law is being broken, there being no air safety inspectors because of the strike in Ontario and Quebec, and because of the safety hazard, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Portage (Mr. Masniuk):
That the Minister of Transport take immediate action to enforce the Aeronautics Act, air regulation-section 400 and that the appropriate action be taken to see that this law is not broken again.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR RECOGNITION OF ABORIGINAL NATIVE RIGHTS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that the Native Council of Canada presented a position paper on aboriginal rights to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the cabinet on April 15, 1975, and in view of the fact that the Prime Minister has not yet responded to the Native Council of Canada position paper although an answer was promised within three months of presentation, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth):
That this House urge the government of Canada to recognize the aboriginal rights of native peoples, including Metis and non-status Indians, and enshrine these rights in the Canadian Constitution in a way which will enable them to preserve and protect their languages and cultures.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF INTERNATIONAL CURRENCY SITUATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I request unanimous consent of the House to present a motion dealing with an important and urgent matter. As the United Kingdom pound has plunged one third in value in the past year, the Italian lira is falling to new lows, while the French franc is under severe pressure, it is urgent that the government inform this House and the Canadian public if any call has been made or any commitment given by Canada to support or indirectly aid any foreign currency and, secondly, review what consequences, if any, may develop in the Canadian economy as a result of this international currency turmoil. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies):
That this important matter be immediately referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs with a view to hearing the Minister of Finance, his officials, the governor of the Bank of Canada, his officials, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, his officials, and other authorities, on the topic and that there be provision for the committee to make recommendations to the government on this subject.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the announcement of dairy policy by the Minister of Agriculture yesterday I will put my question to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and ask him whether he will inform the House why we are faced with the worst of both worlds, namely, an increase in dairy prices to the Canadian consumer at a time when the Minister of Agriculture is asking dairy producers to reduce production?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bryce Mackasey (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Postmaster General
subsubtopic: REASON FOR INCREASE IN PRICE OF DAIRY PRODUCTS
speechtext:
First, allow me to congratulate the hon. gentleman for his new role in the shadow cabinet; I hope he remains in the shadows for a long, long time. As a member who represents a farm region he is in a position to understand the intricacies which have resulted in this situation. The dairy farmers of this country have been victims of a world-wide phenomenon, basically that of a world-wide surplus of skimmed milk powder which has unexpectedly reduced their incomes. Accordingly, all segments of Canadian society have been asked to help the farmers in this situation.
The Treasury Board has aided substantially, farmers themselves are voluntarily cutting down production in this coming year and we have asked the public to absorb 5 cents on the price of butter, knowing full well that if the price of butter continues to rise farmers will eventually see a diminishing market at home, something which would only add to their problems in the long run. I can only hope that the announcement made by the Minister of Agriculture yesterday, with the object of avoiding this situation next year, will have a beneficial effect on prices as well.

us would be selfish enough to share the benefits and not be prepared to share some of the problems of other segments of society. We have helped the dairy farmers, even if the opposition does not agree.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, given the fact that workers in Canada who work for the uranium mines are subject to a totally disproportionate degree of risk of acquiring both silicosis and lung cancer, and given the fact that the trade union negotiating for such employees in the Elliot Lake region negotiated as part of the package an early retirement provision, designed precisely to protect the health of those workers, will the minister assure the House that the government will intervene in the extraordinary decision of the Anti-Inflation Board that held down the proposed negotiated settlement to 12 per cent, the bare guideline in this case, thus putting in total jeopardy the package negotiated by the union, accepted by the company, and intended to protect the health of those employees?

Mr. Speaker, I cannot give the assurance that we will intervene, although my colleague, the Minister of Labour, in particular, has been concerned about the efforts the federal government would like to take to assure better safety standards in uranium mines at Elliot Lake and elsewhere in Canada. I should say that the Anti-Inflation Board will be meeting on Tuesday next, April 20, with parties to this particular settlement for the purpose of clarifying the

decision. I will be looking forward to a report from the board after that time on reactions expressed at that meeting to see what further action might be taken. I might just add in this regard that as soon as Bill C-89 is adopted by the House that would provide a route for either the company or the union to seek a review of the decision. For the time being, the board has agreed to meet with the parties to discuss it further, and I will await the results of that discussion.

speechtext: In light of the fact that this government, as well as the United Nations, has condemned the regime of terror and torture in Chile, and in light of the economic situation there, where there was a 340 per cent inflation rate for 1975, will the minister undertake, as far as he can do so, that the Canadian government will not directly or indirectly support investments by Canadian multinational corporations, which would have the effect of bolstering the regime in Chile?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSALS TO EXTEND COVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement which I hope will be encouraging news to over one half million residents of Canada who are presently deprived of social security benefits earned in other countries because of the absence of reciprocal agreements with those countries.
I wish to announce the government's intention to submit to parliament, in the coming months, legislation amending the Old Age Security Act. Parliament will be asked to
April 14, 1976

adopt measures, first, to increase the flexibility of the residence requirements relating to eligibility for a pension; second, to remove the all-or-nothing feature of the present legislation, thereby relating the pension to the beneficiary's association with Canada and bringing the legislation into line conceptually with the CPP; and third, to build into our program the possibility of its inclusion in international reciprocal arrangements with other countries, such as Italy, the United States, and the United Kingdom, so that our residents who have earned social security rights in foreign countries can receive them in Canada. [Translation]
Canadians haves good reason to be proud of the present old age security program. It is a generous, non-contributory universal program which few other industrialized countries can match. The changes which I propose will not affect the conditions under which lifetime residents of Canada, or those in their immediate pre-retirement years, can qualify for or enjoy their pensions.
Its essential features will remain: universality, payable at age 65, or 60 in the case of the spouse's allowance, eligibility subject to a minimum of ten years residence after age 18 or a minimum of twenty years residence in Canada if it is to be paid on a permanent basis to a beneficiary living abroad. The proposed changes I am announcing today are to enable the program to address the inequities which are arising because of the increasing number of persons whose active working life and retirement are not all spent in Canada. When the program was first introduced, mobility across international boundaries was much less, and migration was usually once-in-a-lifetime event. But the situation is changing and the present act, which takes no account at all of the pension credits which Canadian residents may have acquired in other countries nor provides for international agreements, should also be changed.

These proposals will make the present residence rules fairer and will also make them simpler over the long run. I would like to sketch out the changes and explain our strategy for implementing them.
The government will propose that the old age security pension be "earned" by residents at the rate of one fortieth of the eventual full pension for one year of residence in Canada after age 18. This would mean that legal residence in Canada for 40 years would qualify a person for the full OAS pension, and residence for less than 40 years after age 18 would qualify a person for a portion of the full pension. This change will achieve several worth-while objectives. It will eliminate the inequities which result in a small but significant number of cases from the rigorous application of the current eligibility rules.
At present to qualify for the pension at age 65, one must (a), have resided in Canada for 40 years after age 18 ("40 year rule"); or (b), have resided in Canada for any consecutive 10 year period from age 55 onward ("10 year rule"); or (c), qualify under the "three-for-one rule". This last eligibility rule is a formula under which three years of presence in Canada between age 18 and 55 will count for one year of residence under the ten-year rule provided that the applicant resides in Canada during the year preceding commencement of the pension.
Old Age Security Act
These rules created an all-or-nothing situation. The changes we will propose will relate the amount of the pension to the degree of association that the individual has had with our country. This will create a stronger program, and in fact one which is more consistent with the Canada Pension Plan in which benefits relate to contributions made here.
At the international level the changes which we will be proposing will enhance the government's ability to protect the acquired social security credits of our residents who migrate across international boundaries during their active years, by providing for the negotiation of reciprocal agreements. These would be similar to those already entered into by many countries.
There are a great variety of rules in different countries pertaining to the payment abroad of acquired social security benefits. We will seek enabling amendments to include the OAS program in international social security agreements to be negotiated with other countries. Therefore in addition to the authority which the government presently has to negotiate such agreements in respect to the Canada Pension Plan, we will be proposing to acquire such authority in respect to the Old Age Security Act.
Representations have been made constantly over the years by people who do not receive in Canada payment of pension credits accumulated in their country of origin. I have also received frequent representations concerning this issue from members of all parties, and in particular from members on this side of the House. The proposed amendments should facilitate the payment of such pensions through the negotiation of reciprocal agreements. I am convinced that this measure will be welcomed by the many thousands of Canadians of British, Italian, and other origins. Assuming the co-operation of the foreign governments concerned, it would be our desire to reach early agreements with these countries.
It is our firm intention at the same time to protect those who now have the possibility of eventually qualifying for a full pension under the present rules. Our implementation strategy for the new policy will ensure this. For residents who are 25 or over and in Canada at the time the amendments come into force, the more beneficial set of rules, either the present or new ones, would apply. They too would have the opportunity, as they now have, to qualify for a full pension. This choice of alternatives would also apply to those not now resident in Canada but who have had prior legal residence here after the age of 18. To all others, only the new rules which I have just sketched would apply.
I am announcing our intentions as proposals because I will be consulting with the provinces prior to introducing legislation. I would like, in closing, to ask the unanimous consent of the House to table background information on the matter.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I can have order. What I have to say is for the edification not only of those on this side of the House but those on the other side as well. This statement is obviously a reaction to a bureaucratic oversight and is an attempt to give legitimate power to make international reciprocal agreements, a power that now exists in the Canada Pension Plan. There has now been a recognition of the need of some 500,000 people. It is an astonishing revelation that there are some 500,000 people who are deprived of benefits as a result of the lack of reciprocal agreements. That is the key phrase.
How long has the minister been involved with old age security legislation? Certainly he has since 1973. The act was first brought in in 1951. Now, in 1976, the minister is taking a pie in the sky approach in these proposals, and in the meantime a lot of people are suffering. There has been a cavalier disregard for the plight of thousands of people whose incomes have diminished because of the erosion of the dollar and the high cost of living. Now at long last the government has awakened to the fact that there is significant mobility across international boundaries, and that migration is not a once in a life time matter.
With all respect to the minister, Mr. Speaker, I must say I am somewhat hesitant to give him any praise, even though I like him. He is a nice chap, and although we had a few words of disagreement at the beginning he is trying to do his best. But what disturbs me is the patchwork, ad hoc approach of the minister to our social security programs. At the same time the government is advocating an integrated approach to the entire social security program, and work has been going on now for three years. There is no integration in the minister's proposals; rather it is a patchwork approach that can only lead to further confusion and frustration by denying the rights not of doctors, lawyers, and members of parliament, but of the working poor. This is what I find most discouraging.
We now have a three tiered approach to social security. First there is old age security, and this is going to be affected by the proposed legislation. Old age security is granted universally. We then have the Canada Pension Plan to which a person must contribute. The third tier is private plans. The disturbing thing about private plans is that they are not working. Those who contribute to a private plan are locked in for a 10-year period, and some people leave their employment after five years. I want to know whether the minister is concerned about this. Is he examining the inequities, injustices, and the discrimination that is taking place? I would have thought the minister would have dealt with these questions in his statement.
The minister has now really brought in a fourth tier. The first tier is old age security, the second tier the CPP, and the third private plans. The minister is now taking another approach which puts forward options, and this is why I call it a fourth tier.
April 14, 1976

Let me just refer to what the minister said on page 5 of his statement:
For residents who are 25 or over and in Canada at the time the amendments come into force, the more beneficial set of rules-old or new-would apply. They too would have the opportunity-as they now have-to qualify for a full pension. This choice of alternatives would also apply to those not now resident in Canada but who have had prior legal residence here after the age of 18. To all others, only the new rules which I have just sketched would apply.
What kind of a mess are we getting into, Mr. Speaker? Once again the government is bringing in confusing, frustrating proposals that are extremely complex. I have every sympathy with the minister, but I must inform him that the members on this side, although very sympathetic to the approach to the over-all picture of social security, want something that is easy to understand, not complex, and, unlike what we have now, non-discriminatory.
I note that there are three objectives in the minister's proposals. The first is to increase the flexibility of the residence requirements relating to eligibility for a pension. There is no question that there is a need for equity and fairness in this regard. The second objective is to remove the all or nothing feature of the present legislation, thereby relating the pension to the beneficiary's association with Canada and bringing the legislation into line conceptually with the CPP. I question whether that is fair or just. We are anxious to meet the minister in debate on this floor and in committee so that the many questions that have to be asked can be answered.

I suppose I can say that I have had as much to do with old age pensions over the years as anyone now in this House of Commons, and I take second place to no one in calling for improvements and in pointing out deficiencies and inadequacies.
And the same time, I have to say that in respect of the two matters the minister is now seeking to do something about, his proposals deserve the endorsation of the House. His proposals deal in the main with the residence requirement for old age security on the part of persons who are Canadians, and with the question of reciprocity in the pension field between this country and other countries.
I hope it is not too immodest for me to say that I was asking questions about the residence requirements and pressing for changes at least 30 years ago, and that I started pressing for the government to do something in the field of reciprocity nearly 20 years ago. I recognize that it has taken the government a long time to get to this point, but certainly in the field of reciprocity this does involve negotiations with other countries. Even after this statement the minister may have difficulty achieving as many reciprocal agreements as he would like. So, even though it has taken all this time. I am glad this bit of progress is being made.
I said that the statement deals with two matters: one having to do with reciprocity, and the other having to do with changes in the residence requirements that have to be met in order to qualify for old age security and, consequentially, the guaranteed income supplement.
Despite the fact that my friend who just spoke thinks it is complicated, the general formula that is proposed is better than the one we have now. At the present time we have, as the minister pointed out, the ten-year rule, the 20-year rule, the 40-year rule, the three-for-one-rule, and the last-year rule. It is awfully difficult to explain these

Old Age Security Act
various rules to people. Now we are going to have a rule that says that you earn one fortieth of the old age security pension for each full year you spend in this country as an adult. That will have a particular advantage for persons who spend part of their time in Canada and go to other countries, and it also will have advantage in the long run for those who come from other countries, particularly if reciprocal arrangements can be made with other countries.
Before I go any further in commenting about the new rule, I do hope the minister will let the country know what is happening through the facilities to which he has access. I do hope the press will make the point, and make it absolutely clear, that this change in the legislation does not affect by one cent the pension of any person who is now drawing old age security or the guaranteed income supplement. The minister said that.

speechtext: Anybody who is 25.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSALS TO EXTEND COVERAGE
speechtext:
I will get to that in a moment. The minister said it does not affect anyone who is 25 or over. However, when persons start to hear about the pension being based on the number of years you have been here out of 40 I am sure there will be some senior citizens drawing their pensions, having been here 12, 15 or 20 years, who will wonder whether their pensions are to be reduced. The formula as outlined by the minister says that will not happen. I am satisfied it will not happen and I hope that will be made crystal clear.
The minister has also emphasized by his interruption that neither will this affect anyone in Canada today who is 25 years of age or over. He will have the right if he is not here from 25 to 65 years of age, but meets the other rules, to get the full pension.
The only persons living in Canada who are going to get something less than full pension, that is ten fortieths or twenty fortieths, will be those who come here from other countries. But under the reciprocal arrangements it will be possible for them honestly and openly to receive social security from two countries.
At the present time this matter is abused and is the source of confusion. Some people manage to get old age security in Canada and social security from the United States, going one way or the other. Other people get caught and do not get either, and this is because of the all-or-nothing arrangement, which is now to be changed.
I believe that what is being proposed is something that has been thought out carefully, and something in the long run which will be a lot better. As I say, the provision for basing the pension on the number of years out of 40 that you have been here will make it possible for persons who have been here to age 40 or 50 to go elsewhere and get their share of the Canadian pension along with what they pick up in other countries. It will also be possible for those who come from other countries, under the reciprocal arrangement, to get a total pension income that will be to their advantage. This will be more fair and more equitable, and I congratulate those in the department who have worked this out, and I congratulate the minister for accepting and putting this proposal forward.

At the same time, and even at the risk of saying what the minister thinks he has already said, because people can get concerned and excited, let it be the clearest word that comes out of this House today that no one who is drawing a pension will suffer any loss whatsoever in that pension and that no one who is over 25 years of age will have any different possibility than he now has.
So, Mr. Speaker, I think this will solve many problems. It will certainly get rid of that terribly complex situation we have with the ten, 20, 40, three-for-one, and final year rule. So, in the main I think it is a good arrangement that is being put forward.
If I may go back to the reciprocity question which is half of what is before us today I do urge the government to push this. I know the government has been pushing it for a long time and that other countries have been reluctant to enter into agreements because we were not able to make an agreement involving our old age security.
I know there was the problem when reciprocity was provided in the Canada Pension Plan and not with respect to the Old Age Security Act. This scheme will work satisfactorily and effectively only if we do achieve reciprocal agreements with other countries. The minister mentioned the United Kingdom, Italy, and the United States. I wonder what has happened in respect of the West German situation. I know there is an agreement, but there is much dissatisfaction with it. I hope that that agreement might be renegotiated under the terms of this program. I also notice that France has not been mentioned. I think that is another country with which we should have a reciprocal arrangement.
I press that this be done and that there be pressure to achieve reciprocal agreements because, without this, the whole arrangement has no value for those who come to this country. The new l/40th per year rule is good for Canadians who go elsewhere, because at present they either get all or nothing. But if this legislation is to have advantage for those who come to this country there have to be more reciprocal agreements.
Mr. Speaker, I see you are getting to your favourite position in your chair, at the forward edge. If you sit back I will be through in just a minute. I simply want to say to the minister that although I welcome what he is doing as announced today, I regret that he tells this House he intends to bring in legislation to amend the Old Age Security Act but has not touched on some important issues, namely, the basic amount of the old age security which should be increased substantially, and the question of the eligible age which, in my view, should be 60 for all those who are out of the labour market. Neither has he told us what he intends to do about the discrimination in respect of the spouses' legislation against spinsters, widows, bachelors and widowers, and I hope that when he gets around to bringing in this legislation these shortcomings will be corrected. It is fine to have the improvements which are proposed today, but surely when the minister brings in the actual bill he will have in it some of the substantial improvements that are needed with regard to senior citizens in Canada right now.
April 14, 1976

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSALS TO EXTEND COVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall do my best not to abuse your patience. However, I would like to thank the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) who in today's statement informed us that amendments will soon be made to the Old Age Security Act to allow greater continuity of old age protection by transferability of acquired credit, through the agreements that he will be able to negotiate and ratify with other governments.
I agree with the minister that the present plan lacks flexibility. This is what my party has always maintained. In the field of old age and social security, there is also a lack of flexibility, as in the income security system, which is outdated. This is why we have long urged the minister to consider seriously the very simple non-bureaucratic and less costly formula of a guaranteed annual income, which would allow each Canadian citizen to be spared the problems of an increasingly costly and inefficient bureaucracy.
Instead of aiming at gradually correcting the present income security program in general, which includes the old age security program, the minister would have advantage, so as to present a comprehensive guaranteed annual income program and improving at the same time the old age security program, the minister, as I say, would have advantage to consider more seriously our proposal so that all Canadians can be ensured of a guaranteed annual income and an old age security pension.
The minister has informed us that 500,000 Canadians are now deprived of benefits which they could receive from other countries and a great number of Canadians who have emigrated abroad cannot receive benefits concerning security of foreigners. This is what caused the minister to propose today amendments which will eventually rectify this situation. When the amendments are introduced, we shall be able to study the proposals in detail, but we still want to thank the minister for having at least taken one step forward in this area today, since, according to what he said, at least 500,000 Canadians cannot receive their old age security pension under the present Old Age Security Act.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSALS TO EXTEND COVERAGE
speechtext:
Order, please. The procedure which we have been following in respect of ministerial statements calls for a statement by the minister and then brief responses by members of the opposition. The response from the last member of the opposition, the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau), was indeed in keeping with those guidelines. The response from the first two spokesmen for the opposition parties was uniformly about twice the length of the minister's statement. I did not intervene, but at this point it is an exercise of my discretion under these practices as to what questions should be allowed.
Bearing in mind those speeches, and also bearing in mind the fact that the purpose of the statement is an announcement of the introduction of legislation which will be coming before the House at another time when there will be a response to questions, I really think that I should extend questions only to allow the minister to make some retaliation to some of the things that have been said about him during the course of the comments. Perhaps one
Old Age Security Act
spokesman for each party would be more than adequate under the circumstances.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I accept your admonishment and will try to be as responsible as I can. I shall ask as few questions as possible in the knowledge that we will be getting the legislation.
I should just like to ask the minister some questions regarding the reciprocal agreements, which is a subject with which we have all been involved, particularly in respect of the United Kingdom. I know I have been involved with it since 1973. I think the step that is being taken certainly is in the right direction. The minister mentioned the United States, the United Kingdom, and Italy. What are the other countries to which he is now directing his attention in terms of agreement, so that we can have something on the record in that regard?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSALS TO EXTEND COVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the countries which have been most persistent and pressing in terms of reaching an agreement are the three countries I have mentioned. We already have an agreement with Germany. That is open for revision if the legislation is passed. Obviously France also would be a natural candidate for negotiation.
Frankly it is a matter of dealing with priorities. I must say that the cases of the United Kingdom, Italy, and the United States have been the ones that have been most urgent. However, we will proceed in respect of any country that is ready and willing to sit down and start negotiations.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will just leave that. I think the minister has answered it adequately for the time being. What about consultation with the provinces? I am wondering whether the minister has had some agreement. Is there some unanimity concerning this particular proposal and will there be an opting out formula in respect of it? Is it a shared cost program?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSALS TO EXTEND COVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there seems to be a slight misunderstanding as to the meaning of the consultation with the provinces. However, before I answer that I might add with respect to the previous question that we will carry on with these foreign countries the exploratory talks that we have been having for the past couple of years in some instances.
Obviously if we cannot find agreement we cannot make anything formal until the law is amended, but we are open for exploratory talks at the present time. So far as the consultation is concerned, this type of amendment does not require consent in respect of anything over which any province has any veto. It does not imply participation as such by the provinces. It is more a matter of courtesy and common sense, since we are discussing the whole field of social security, that I should have a word with them to see whether they have any specific concern with regard, for instance, to some aspects that might have some implications for social assistance, and about which they might want to draw specific points to my attention.
In addition, the fact is that this type of amendment will facilitate reciprocal agreements with other countries. It

April 14, 1976
Old Age Security Act
will be easier to achieve these agreements if we can include Workmen's Compensation which is under provincial jurisdiction, as well as other federal programs, so this is the purpose of the consultation. The purpose is not to give the provinces a right of veto over our formal approval of these proposals, but to ensure that these amendments will be harmonized with whatever the provinces are doing at their own level.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSALS TO EXTEND COVERAGE
speechtext: The minister has answered the question that there is need for provincial consultation and that it will be high on the priority list. I have just one last question. I am a little confused. Suppose someone comes from Italy and someone comes from the United Kingdom, and they are both eligible under the new legislation. If Italy has no reciprocal agreements with Canada but the United Kingdom has, then one of the two people, regardless of his eligibility, will be denied his benefits because his country has no reciprocal agreement. Is that how it will work?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSALS TO EXTEND COVERAGE
speechtext:
Yes, the hon. member understands it correctly. In that sense, I could go back to something he said about the half a million people who are not enjoying the full benefits which they have earned in the foreign countries. The proposed amendments will not guarantee to them that they will receive such benefits because we obviously cannot legislate for foreign countries. But we will do everything we can in terms of our own legislation and in terms of opening the doors for negotiations and agreements to ensure a reciprocity of benefits so that there will be what we call prorating and totalization of benefits, both those earned here, and those earned abroad.
Obviously, if a foreign country does not want to pay such pension credits to its former citizens, there is not much Canada can do. In fact, there is nothing preventing any of those countries from paying those benefits at the present time to the roughly 500,000 residents of Canada of whom we spoke, and there is nothing in the present Canadian legislation that would prevent this from taking place. However, those countries are saying that they will not pay unless they have an agreement.
Since our system is based on an all or nothing formula, they say that since we are paying a full pension by Canadian standards, why should they pay anything. That is the situation at present. What we are proposing is to make it much easier for these foreign governments to start paying pensions to their former residents who have earned them abroad in Canada.

consultation, not a case of their approval having to be obtained. In doing that he referred to such things as workmen's compensation being in the total picture of reciprocity. I can get all my questions in at once, unless something comes out of what the minister says. The big question is, when will this legislation be introduced?

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSALS TO EXTEND COVERAGE
speechtext:
In answer to the first question, I am not aware of current negotiations taking place with any of the countries which the hon. member has mentioned. Obviously we are open to such negotiations, but I am not aware that there are such active negotiations at present.
With regard to the second point, when this matter was considered, it was obviously considered by cabinet and all the ministers involved, including the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald). In the course of our negotiations we will take into account all the federal programs which include the possibility of reciprocal agreements such as the Unemployment Insurance Act which has provisions in that respect. We hope to be able to put in the basket all the various federal programs in the field of social security that provide for reciprocal agreements.
Finally, there is the question of when this legislation will be introduced. I hope to introduce it as early as possible during the course of the next session. I would like to be told that there is a possibility that it could be passed before June 30, but knowing what is on the agenda and the difficulty of getting it through the House, I am skeptical that it can be introduced before the fall.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very surprised that the acting government House leader has not seen fit to get up on this motion and defend the record of the government.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Perhaps the reason he did not get up and defend it is that he is basically an honest man, and when he looked at the record he really had nothing to defend.
What really does surprise me is the courage of the government in deciding to adjourn the House today. This motion, unless hon. members opposite hive themselves off in their hotel rooms and in their offices, will set them out in the streets, highways and byways of their constituencies to meet the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: They are anxious to see us.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am sure hon. members opposite are anxious to see the people, and I am sure the people of Canada are anxious to see them, to ask them what has gone wrong with the ship of state here in Ottawa and why the government is shambling and moving seemingly without rudders or leadership with respect to all kinds of matters.
While it has always been the usual attitude of the opposition to fight adjournment and to make the government stay and tackle the problems for which governments are basically responsible because of their own neglect and dereliction, our attitude today will be a little different because we feel it is a good thing for this complex of dispensables, this shambling group which masquerades as a government, to go out and meet those for whom they say they speak. They pound their desks and say aye when the time comes to say aye, and nay when the time comes to say nay. I think that group which masquerades as a government should go out and meet the people of this country and find out just what the people really think of their performance.

It would ruin their holiday.
Easter Adjournment

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like us to consider for a moment the members of the government. Let us think about the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). This morning in the Globe and Mail someone called him a "dyed in the bull" politician. Let us think about what he did. He carried off a masterpiece today and yesterday with respect to the dairy policy he introduced. He managed to do what no other minister of agriculture has ever been able to do, and that is shaft both producers and consumers at the same time. That takes some doing.
That is known as the Whelan principle.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Perhaps it is known as the Whelan principle. It is not the principle of relativity, in any event.
Then there is the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), who has no energy and who is prepared to let the Atlantic provinces heat and light themselves "at twice the price."
The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) is the minister who has forgotten that when you build jails and penitentiaries you are supposed to put locks on the doors to keep the inmates in. He has forgotten the problems which are faced by his own staff. He has been condemned by the leadership of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. When I think of the morale of the RCMP, the morale of the people who work in our prisons and the dreadful conditions in them- if we believe half of what we are told, and I suggest we can believe at least that-I wonder why the minister should be in that portfolio at all. I wonder why he should be supported. If hon. members cf the government are going to speak today, they should tell us why the Solicitor General should be supported, except that he happens to be one of their own.
If there is any situation in Canada which needs a clear investigation by someone who is prepared to look at all sides of the issue, it is the situation in our penitentiaries and the situation with regard to the RCMP, to which the government is prepared to give lip service, but in terms of the rumblings of discontent within that latter service there is an indication that something is wrong, and I suggest something is wrong with the government, not just with the Solicitor General. Surely the shoulders of the Solicitor General are not broad enough to bear all the results of the acts of omission and commission of the government.
If this is the season of tranquility and peace, I think we should leave this House and hope that in the spirit of Easter we might see a government returned refreshed. But I do not think there is very much left to refresh in terms of this government. With such a ministry is it any wonder that this country is in such difficulty?
[DOT] <1610)
Can any good Liberal be proud of the government's legislative accomplishments? What have hon. members opposite contributed to debates in this House? What has been the contribution of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale), apart from the occasional reply? For most part it has consisted of "Oh, oh!" or "Hear, hear!" Is it any wonder our people question the wisdom of the government? We are going through an economic crisis, a crisis

April 14, 1976
Easter Adjournment
involving the Solicitor General's department, and a crisis relating to the government's moral and ethical standards.
What standards?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Apparently, in matters of ministerial ethics, the government considers the Criminal Code as the basic guide, not the guidelines set down by Lester B. Pearson. As the ship of state plows ahead, bumping a shoal here and a shoal there, with nobody at the helm, is it any wonder people think the government is a drifting mess.
In his year-end oration the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said parliament is irrelevant. The people of this country now think the Prime Minister himself is irrelevant. I ask hon. members to cast their minds back. When, in modern parliamentary history, have two ministers submitted their resignations in such circumstances as we witnessed? When has it ever happened that one resignation was accepted, and one not accepted on such specious grounds? When has a ministry been involved with matters like Sky Shops, the dial-a-judge affair and other, similar matters which have come before the House?
If government supporters are dismayed by opposition charges, I merely say that the opposition cannot make bricks without straw. The actions of the government, or its lack of action and-I use the word in its parliamentary sense-the wrongful acts of the government and those beholden to it have created the straw. We merely brought these matters to the attention of the House. When did you ever see such evasion? Certainly not in my time here. Perhaps others, who have been here longer, remember similar instances, but I do not.
When did you ever see such posturing as went on in the last year and a half, such empty posturing? Why, it has become necessary for the government to invent reasons for avoiding the public inquiries which we asked. Only when those involved in the matter were not in the government or closely connected with it was an inquiry granted. Otherwise, when we have asked for people unbiased politically to inquire into important public matters, we have been refused and stonewalled. Other times the government asked us to lay charges; but the government would not provide information which would allow us to make a judgment. Government members have tried to intimidate opposition members in a question period, and failed. This government has much to account for to the people of this country.
Why is the government afraid to face the people of Canada? The Prime Minister spurned the invitation to face the public in St. John's West, until he could spurn it no longer. We shall know the people's answer to the government when the people of St. John's West speak. Yes, the Prime Minister will have his birthday present in October, 1976. And what is to happen in Ottawa-Carleton? How can the Prime Minister justify leaving over 100,000 people in Ottawa-Carleton without representation in this House? Why has he refused, despite the pressure put on him by the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and other opposition members, to say when an ordinary process in a democratic society is to take place, namely, a by-election?

The Ottawa Journal, a newspaper known for its unbiased approach to public matters-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: -said, in an editorial printed on April 12, 1976-
It's about as unbiased as the Daily Worker.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
-as follows:
Of course no justification is possible. Mr. Trudeau is willingly sacrificing the interests of parliamentary democracy for the perceived selfinterest of the Liberal party. His political advisers are worried about an Ottawa-Carleton by-election, as well they should be. The delay in even announcing its date is entirely for partisan reasons.
Before Mr. Trudeau next talks about the irrelevancy of parliament, he might contemplate his own contribution to that sad fact.
With every passing day the government exposes its weakness. Although ministers demonstrate their technical knowledge and managerial ability, their credibility inexorably is lessened. The government is becoming less and less realistic in its assessment of the problems we all face. A government like that should go out to the people of Canada-
It should go out, period.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) says, it should go out. And I do not want anyone to think that the government neglects only the big issues. It neglects the small ones as well. In all aspects of its activities it has demonstrated the same inability, incompetence, and disregard for matters small as well as large.
I allude particularly to a matter I raised the other day as a point of order. Mr. Speaker decided that it was not a point of order, but I suggest that it concerned the smirking hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) and others, as it has to do with the position of parliamentary secretary. A section of the Parliamentary Secretaries Act provides that:
There shall not be at any one time more parliamentary secretaries than the number of ministers who hold offices for which salaries are provided in section 4 of the Salaries Act.
This subsection refers to the ministers in office and not to the total number of eligible portfolios. We have, by virtue of the Government Reorganization Act, provision-for a total of 28 full ministers and, therefore, a possible 28 parliamentary secretaryships. This government has not appointed an associate minister of national defence. It only takes one minister of national defence to foul up the defence posture of the country. We do not need an associate minister. Prior to March 16 there were 27 full ministers and 27 parliamentary secretaries. The three ministers of state do not enter into these calculations because they do not fall within the definition.
When the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) resigned as minister of consumer and corporate affairs, there remained 26 ministers drawing salaries pursuant to section 4 of the Salaries Act. As a consequence there is one parliamentary secretary too many in terms of salary. There are some in this country who would say there are 20 odd
April 14, 1976

parliamentary secretaries too many in terms of the work they do. However, I am not going to raise that matter in this debate.
On Thursday, April 8, the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) was given the additional portfolio of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. He has proved that he cannot run the Post Office. He is now going to prove that he cannot run that department. Consequently there is a minister for each of the 27 portfolios. However, there are still only 26 ministers holding an office for which a salary is provided for a parliamentary secretary. Since the number of ministers is operative in determining the number of parliamentary secretaries, there is still one parliamentary secretary too many as of this time. It appears that one parliamentary secretary is drawing his salary illegally.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: None of them earn the salary, but one is drawing it illegally. I raise this with the government and I was thanked by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Blais) for doing so. I want to know which one of the parliamentary secretaries is going to volunteer not only to give up the salary but to send back vyhat he has taken from the Crown improperly.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
As I said, Mr. Speaker, the government provides an equal amount of neglect to each problem facing it. The parliamentary secretaries must be delighted to know that they are among the small problems. However, their neglect in this problem is very important in terms of proper administration under the statute. But the government ignores the problem.
We do not resist too strenuously adjournment at this time. In order for the government members to have more than a short exposure to the people on the streets of Canada we might increase the number of days. However, there will at least be time for them to understand fully that outside this lovely precinct of parliament, insulated as it is from time to time from what people on the street are saying, there are a great number of Canadians who look upon the government with the same disdain and disgust as many members of this House of Commons.
There are problems in Canada. There are great challenges facing the country. Frankly I do not believe that this shambling, dried-up bureaucratic, technocratic government, which once classed its members as great managers, is capable of managing its own affairs, let alone the affairs of a country that requires a unique kind of attention.
It would be very well if this House were dissolved and we went to the country. If this were the case today, there would be no doubt about the outcome. I would be immodest if I suggested that we might have an opportunity to go across the floor of the House, so I will not suggest it. I would rather say that members opposite will have an opportunity to test the other side of the House. With the situation in this country, this could not happen too soon. I
Easter Adjournment
do not know how long any country can withstand the neglect and lack of policy and direction. This government has ably demonstrated its incapability.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, if Canadians picked at random a group of people to run the government and sit in the cabinet, they would come up with a group that in the normal course of time would make a number of decisions which would include some good results and some errors. However, it is a marvellous accomplishment of this collection of Liberals to turn virtually every aspect of policy that they have had to deal with since the Christmas break into an unmitigated disaster. No other group of Canadians could have been so successful at spoiling virtually everything they touched in terms of policy in the past few months.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), on behalf of the government, moved a motion of adjournment. We all noticed that he did not say anything. I do not mean that in the normal Liberal sense where they speak at length without any substance, but in the literal sense in that he simply moved the motion and resumed his seat. The reason is obvious. He would have had to speak in terms of pure hypocrisy about the record of the government, or tell the truth. If he chose the latter he would not have anything to say of a positive nature about the performance of the government.
In the past three months we have had the worst consecutive period of government for a three month period in the living memory of any member in this chamber.
Even Stanley!

We had the judges' affair and the Sky Shops' affair. The over-riding conclusion that has to be drawn from these two episodes is that, apart from the Criminal Code, the government has absolutely no standards. If it is not illegal, for a Liberal it is permitted, unless he is caught. If caught, the principle is that they do their damndest to cover it up. If they are caught trying to cover it up, they get some minister to resign for a completely phony reason and hope that no one will notice. That is the standard this cabinet has set in the last three months. I have no doubt that it has contributed to its very significant nosedive in the Gallup poll figures recently announced.
There has been a total abandonment of the serious parliamentary tradition, both in this country and abroad, that ministers have moral responsibilities that are well above those provided in the Criminal Code. Long after the temporary illustrations of the so-called judges' affair and the Sky Shops' issue are forgotten, neither of which is comp-letedly resolved by a long shot, the permanent effect upon the government and the Liberal party will be that the people of Canada will judge them as a party that looks upon this nation in a completely cynical fashion, a fashion which states that, as long as it is not illegal, it is to be permitted. That is a standard that all parties on the opposition side made clear in the past few weeks that they categorically reject.

Hear, hear!

April 14, 1976
Easter Adjournment

As for the Defence Department, I do not know if one could get lower in any provincial or federal department, in this country or anywhere else. The $1 billion misunderstanding with regard to the Orion is almost beyond description in terms of the incompetency of the government. It is an incredible mishandling of public responsibility and public funds. All opposition parties have played a role in showing that this profound mishandling is taking place in the Defence Department by the current minister.
We are spending $1 billion on Lockheed Orions, which I suggest are not going to serve the first priority of our defence, as stated by the government itself in its 1971 defence white paper, namely, the protection and enhancement of Canadian sovereignty. We are spending millions of dollars on needlessly complex, technical equipment for the Orion, which the minister acknowledged in committee and acknowledged implicitly in the House has no other purpose but to provide the technical capacity to detect submarines in the course of supplying protective coverage for convoys carrying goods back and forth across the Atlantic in the event of a prolonged land war in continental Europe.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, could anyone other than the present Minister of Defence (Mr. Richardson) come up with such a hypothetical possibility in the year 1976 which has such absurd implications? As I said on another occasion, in the Orion deal the minister has prepared magnificently for refighting the second world war. This can be facetiously or jokingly dismissed, but we are not approaching it in that way, Mr. Speaker. Defence spending is a serious matter.
However, there is yet hope. The deal is not settled. We have suggested that the government extricate itself completely from the Lockheed deal and proceed to purchase and build planes in Canada. The Dash 7-R can be built in Canada, and given the right kind of equipment can undertake the surveillance task which, I repeat, was the number one task assigned to the defence department in the government's white paper. This can be supplemented by re-equipping the Argus aircraft, which can provide surveillance for submarines along our coast where this is appropriate. This would leave some $500 million which could be used for sensible, long-range purposes. For example, it could be used to develop inter-urban rapid transit facilities, which also can be produced in Canada and would meet Canada's urban needs.
As for inflation and unemployment, I will not go back over the origin of the anti-inflation program that was presented to the House shortly after last Thanksgiving. If one looks at what has transpired since we returned to the House following the Christmas recess, the weakness of the program in terms of its legal structure, complemented by regulations and administrative decisions, have more than confirmed our original conclusion about the program, namely, that it was primarily a wage and salary control program and not at all a price control program.
Perhaps the symbolic appointment that best characterizes the fact that the government was not serious about prices was the appointment of a man named Lasby as head of the profit control section of the Anti-Inflation Board

administrative apparatus concerned with food prices. Did the government appoint a social worker, a trade unionist, a fisherman, or an ordinary worker to this position, Mr. Speaker? No, it wanted someone Very dear to the hearts of the Liberal party and hired Mr. Lasby, who was formerly vice-president of Canada Packers. Mr. Lasby would know very well about price fixing and how the system works, but he would not be the kind of person in terms of disposition to look for profiteering and price gouging, which surely should have been the sort of person the government was seeking for this particular role in its anti-inflation program.
Perhaps it is just a mere coincidence that the board has rolled back in more than five months of existence only one price increase in Canada, and that was the price of a particular brand of beer manufactured in the province of Quebec. Some record indeed! In the meantime the board has rolled back some 100 trade union contracts and wage and salary settlements. The board has before it some 6,000 contracts, and since the program began has reached a decision on 2,000 of them. Some 4,000 remain. But overwhelmingly the emphasis of the board has been on rolling back contracts that have been negotiated and settled by the participants, not in any circumstance on improving those settlements.
The legislation that we have passed dealing with inflation was anti-working Canadian at its inception and has remained anti-working Canadian in its application. The recent cost of living figures illustrate this. There was a slight decline in the cost of living, but contrary to what certain government members have said this reduction was not at all the result of the anti-inflation program. This reduction occurred in sectors that the program does not control, namely, imported goods and food prices. The fact of the matter is that the most important price increases for Canadians are not covered by the program. I will not go into them at length but simply mention them: energy prices, mortgage costs, and food prices. These are virtually exempt in the most important respects from the anti-inflation program, yet they are most relevant to the budget of a typical family.
Another area that the government has fouled up-and I think that is the appropriate term-has been federal-provincial relations. In the last few months the government has reneged on a whole range of programs originally negotiated between the Government of Canada and the provinces during the last few years. This is the case particularly in regard to those programs involving the transfer of financial resources from the federal government to some of the provinces, which inescapably has normally meant the transfer of wealth from the wealthier provinces to the poorer. As I say, the federal government has reneged on the agreements it entered into with the provinces ostensibly in good faith. Now the financial burden has got a little tough, the federal government has turned its back.
This is particularly so in the case of health care financing, and it has had a very bad effect on the poorer provinces. The same is true of the revenue guarantee agreements entered into with the provinces some five years ago. The federal government's unilateral and arbitrary action in these areas not only jeopardizes the good relationships that are essential between the federal government and the
April 14, 1976

provinces, but it has had a negative effect in terms of the income benefits of our citizens. In all these instances it means that the poorer provinces of Canada are going to suffer and become even poorer.
Again the government's lack of action and failure to take specific steps is seen in its treatment of the native peoples of this country. Tomorrow is the first anniversary of a special submission on the aboriginal rights of Metis and non-status Indians made to the cabinet, and specifically to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), by the Native Council of Canada. At that time the Native Council of Canada was promised a response by the government within three months. That is a year ago tomorrow. I say with all seriousness that if the Government of Canada does not act, and act soon in terms of the needs and the aboriginal rights of the native people of Canada, we will experience a very significant, and I will not put it more strongly than that, level of civil disobedience in this country. It may well go beyond that, the issue is that serious.
A government that promises a year ago that it will act within three months and has yet done nothing is not a government that deserves the support either of the native people of Canada or of the rest of us. Our party believes it is time the rights of the native people of Canada were guaranteed. We believe their linguistic and cultural rights should be guaranteed in precisely the same way as the linguistic and cultural rights of French and English-speaking people are guaranteed. By that we mean they should be firmly embedded in our constitution. That is what they want, and it is time the Government of Canada gave recognition to the desire and implemented it.
Another area in respect of which the government can be criticized with complete justification is that of its neglect of women's rights. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) put on one fancy and expensive fanfare after another, along with a little bit of showbiz here at the National Arts Centre and its equivalent in Winnipeg, where there was a great production with buttons and everything, all during International Women's Year. Once the great and symbolic year was over we got no action at all.
There was a possibility within the anti-inflation program of making it clear that the women of Canada who still experience wage and salary discrimination ought not, in terms of the law, be subject to a continuation of that discrimination. The normal cop-out of the federal government was the suggestion that these people are employed within the framework of provincial law. That was the government's excuse up to its new anti-inflation law. Now that this has been brought in under the guise and within the framework of exceptional constitutional powers given to the federal government in emergency situations, the peace, order and good government clause, the government no longer has that excuse. While this legislation is on the books it provides the government with a perfect opportunity to practise this year what it preached last year when it was fashionable to talk about women's rights. It could have made it mandatory that women in Canada in the market place be paid on a full equality basis.
Easter Adjournment
Another area the government has been treating with blase indifference is that area of the automotive industry in Canada. This is a serious part of our industry, and in the province of Ontario alone one out of six jobs is directly or indirectly related to it. The government has been sitting waiting month after month, indeed, year after year in recent years, while our relative position compared to the United States automotive industry has gone down.
Last year we had a $2 billion deficit in automotive trade with the United States. That's a lot of dollars, and this affects our trade position seriously. It is also translatable into jobs. That means a lot of men and women in this country have been unemployed who might otherwise have been employed. If the trend which I understand has taken place during the first two months of this year persists, I predict that the deficit for 1976 will likely reach $3 billion. I understand we have a deficit not only in the automotive parts sector, which has been traditional over the years, but also unfortunately we have a deficit in the assembly sector in trade with the United States. I predict this with care, and with some knowledge about this industry.
It is time the Government of Canada recognized the importance of what is taking place within the framework of the Canada-U.S. automotive agreement and took steps to change it so Canadians would get, not more than their share, but at least their share in terms of jobs that were supposed to be guaranteed by that pact. In addition, the Canadian consumers would get the benefits they were supposed to get when the tax came into being ten years ago, namely, price parity in automotive production. They do not get this and, in fact, this is just as bad today as it was in 1965 when the pact came into being.
The final matter I wish to mention that is of concern to us is the decision that is likely to be reached in cabinet tomorrow concerning drilling in the Beaufort Sea. This is another example of the government plunging ahead without any thought about the consequences when it gave approval in principle to Dome Petroleum in 1973 starting some preliminary drilling there. In spite of requests from the United States government to delay, in spite of the expressed concern by the federal Department of the Environment, which has pointed out that if a blow-out occurs in the Beaufort Sea it could run wild for up to two years, and particularly in spite of the opposition by the United States government to proceeding so quickly, the government gives every indication that it will decide to proceed with that operation.
We in the NDP assert that this is a wrong decision. The technology being used, to our knowledge, is not sufficient to guarantee the kind of environmental safety that is essential. We say the decision should be delayed and that this action should not go ahead. I repeat that all the indicators seem to be that the government will proceed, as soon as it gets the opposition parties out of Ottawa, with that very important and potentially very harmful decision.
