speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address myself very briefly to one question that has been raised repeatedly during this session, and certainly during the 1976 portion, and this relates to search and rescue.
Since January we have lost six fishermen off the coast of Newfoundland and four fishermen off the coast of British Columbia. In March the fisheries patrol vessel Cape Friels went down leaving 23 men in the water for 15 hours. It was just by a very happy coincidence that at that particular time there happened to be a tracker aircraft from Halifax on the ground in St. John's. That tracker aircraft was able to get in the air and succeeded in locating these men. We are told they were within one hour of being lost because of a developing weather system in the area. I am further told that the pilot of that tracker aircraft was severely reprimanded by his superiors for refusing to obey orders and insisting on staying over the area until the rescue vessel was in sight. As I say, that would have been a very serious disaster indeed.
It came as no surprise when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) issued a statement on April 7 under the heading "Marine Search and Rescue (SAR) Activities". This was an eight-page resume of the inventory of the Canadian coast guard. The minister really did not address himself to the total search and rescue effort. What really surprised me and most people was the very dramatic admission on page eight of that statement. This is what the Minister of Transport said:
It has become evident that, in spite of the provision of additional resources, facilities and coordination capabilities over the years, the marine SAR organization is no longer entirely adequate.
That is precious little consolation to the families of those fishermen who have been lost this year. Then the minister went on to state:
A Canadian Coast Guard Task Force has reviewed the national search and rescue policy and the revised policy is expected to be ready for submission to Cabinet by mid-1976.
The Minister of Transport accused me of misreading his statement. He said his statement referred to the report being ready before mid-summer 1976. That is what Hansard will show. I hope the parliamentary secretary will note that the statement of April 7 said that the submission would not be ready until mid-summer 1976.
This is a most crucial fact. It raises the whole question that, once the Minister of Transport arrives at the point in time where he is ready to admit what we have been saying all along, which is that the present search and rescue facilities are not adequate, it then becomes incumbent upon the minister and his colleagues in cabinet to assure

the House and the Canadian people that an interim measure is being put into effect which would cover, on an interim basis, the inadequacies referred to by the minister in his statement, at least until the task force makes its report by mid-summer.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, this is a most grievous thing because we are about to embark upon another fishing season on the east coast of Canada. I believe the minister has put himself in the position by that admission that, if there is another accident at sea involving Canadian fishermen, which by the very nature of the occupation there probably will be, God forbid, the government will be condemned by its own words. This government by its own admission places itself in the position of being accused of what to my mind is tantamount to criminal negligence.
I do not know what the legal position will be if there should be another accident at sea either on the east coast or on the west coast, but certainly we have a right to expect from the minister some assurance that the inadequacies which obviously have been identified will be corrected, at least on an interim basis, to ensure maximum efficiency during the crucial time when the task force is preparing its report, which report will not be ready for submission to cabinet until mid-summer, or perhaps even later.
The last tragedy at sea in my province was the floundering of the fishing vessel the San Juan with the loss of two lives. My question today to the minister was whether or not he is now prepared, in light of the submission of the report by his department into the sinking of the San Juan, to have a full scale judicial inquiry. I submit such an inquiry is warranted by the tabling in this House by the minister of the in-house inquiry report of his department.
Such an inquiry is warranted because, according to this report, only the captain of the CGS Bartlett and only the first officer of the vessel and the quartermaster were interviewed. Why were the members of the RCMP not interviewed since they were instrumental in notifying the air-sea search and rescue in Halifax that the San Juan was lost? Second, why were not the personnel of the air-sea search and rescue in Halifax not interviewed to determine what procedure was taken immediately following the receipt of this news?
What seems to be perhaps even more difficult to understand is why were not the members of the crew of the Bartlett who were on deck at the time not interviewed by this inquiry or investigation? I say, Sir, that unfortunately, because I am sure this was the conclusion of well meaning people, this investigation raises more questions than it answers. I find one part of the report particularly objectionable. On page three of the report there is a reference to the fact that the two fishermen, Mr. Coady and Mr. Ryan were on some kind of pleasure cruise. The suggestion was made that they were out sports fishing, that they were shooting birds for sport.
The Newfoundland fishermen do not venture out into the North Atlantic in the middle of February for sport. They do so because that is a crucial part of their existence. They do so for the very important reason that they have to supplement their inadequate incomes. They supplement their income by catching a few fish for their table or by shooting some seabirds to provide some fresh meat. That
April 14, 1976

has been the traditional pattern of Newfoundland fishermen. It is unworthy of the people who prepared that report, and of the Minister of Transport who presented it, to suggest that these two fishermen who were lost were out on some kind of sporting venture.
I wonder whether the Minister of Transport would have the courage to go to the widow of one of these fishermen and adviser her and her nine children that the husband and father was lost while on a sporting cruise on that ill-fated day. How many more fishermen will have to be lost before this government gets the message that it has an on-going responsibility to protect Canadians at sea and in the air?
I venture to say that if some kook were to take it upon himself to cross the Atlantic in a balloon, as has happened on a number of occasions, and if by the very nature of that foolhardy exercise was to come down somewhere in the northwest Atlantic, the full capability of Canada's search and rescue and of the United States search and rescue facilities would be brought to bear to save the skin of that nut. Yet, Sir, we seem to be suggesting that if fishermen engage in some kind of sporting pastime with their equipment while waiting for the fishing season to commence, or if fishermen on the west coast of Canada venture out without adequate equipment, then somehow they are not entitled to the same protection as they would were they engaged in legitimate fishing activity.
I submit that all Canadians involved in fishing, be it sport or otherwise, are entitled to the protection that is their right as Canadian citizens. That is why I believe, with the admission of the Minister of Transport that the present procedures are inadequate, with the further admission that the task force report will not be ready until mid-summer, that we must have some assurance that steps will be taken in the interim to correct the inadequacies.
The minister in the report on the San Juan incident made no reference to the air-sea rescue Centre in Halifax or the responsibilities they have. The report carried with it the implication that there is a division of responsibility here which all too often has resulted in a very serious loss of time in getting the search and rescue in operation.
On the one hand we are told that the Department of Transport is responsible for the marine capability in search and rescue, and on the other the Department of National Defence is responsible for the air capability. That is not my understanding of it. My understanding of it is that the Department of National Defence, which operates the four search and rescue centres in Canada, is responsible for the over-all supervision of search and rescue in Canada. It is its responsibility to take the initiative. Indeed the initiative cannot be taken unless the air-sea rescue centres have been notified, and indeed air-sea rescue centres have the ongoing co-ordinating responsibility once a search gets under way.
Yet we have all these contradictions creeping in from time to time. For example, General Dextrase when he was before the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence on March 23, in his statement, which can be found in the report of the committee of that day, said:
Easter Adjournment
But I do believe the responsibility is not ours. I do not want to sound callous; somebody has to do the job. But if we are forever coming back when we are discussing estimates and having the Department of National Defence picking up whatever is alleged or considered as not being done by anyone else, then the budget will certainly have to include it.
Obviously the Commanding General of the Canadian Armed Forces does not have the same understanding of the division of responsibility that the Minister of Transport and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) have. I would say that we deserve, the people of Canada deserve, and certainly our fishermen deserve, to know exactly what interim measures the government will take to correct the inadequacies identified by the minister in his statement last week. We deserve that because, after all, if a municipality is about to acquire a new fire engine, it does not close down the fire hall because the existing equipment is inadequate. It takes whatever steps are necessary to bring the present equipment up to maximum efficiency on an interim basis until the new equipment is ready, and certainly that applies with a great deal of force and legitimacy to the whole question of air-sea rescue.
I will not take too much of the time of the House, but in conclusion I want to make reference to the report of Judge Soper who headed a judicial inquiry into the loss of the fishing vessel Enterprise, and the foundering of the Canadian National ship Patrick Morris which was engaged in the search of the Enterprise in 1970. Judge Soper released his report in 1971 and identified the problem. For example, he said:
There is one factor which should be examined by the appropriate authorities of the Government of Canada and that is the "reaction time", which is the time lag between the order to go on a mission and the take-off of aircraft.
I did some checking today with the Canadian Armed Forces and I am told that the tracker aircraft, a prop aircraft which is the kind of equipment we now have, takes approximately three and a half hours flying time to get from Halifax to eastern Newfoundland. That is a critical time factor. As I mentioned earlier, it is only by the grace of God that there was a tracker at St. John's at the time the Cape Freels was lost because, if that tracker had not been there, we would probably have been faced with a tragedy of huge proportions in that 23 men would have been lost. Yet we had to depend on the east coast of Newfoundland on an air element that is operational from Halifax or Summerside, Prince Edward Island.
What did Judge Soper have to say about that in his report? He made some important recommendations which, to the best of my knowledge, have never been acted upon. That report was handed down in 1971. In addition to addressing himself to the critical time lag he recommended that there should be greater dispersal, greater deployment of air-sea rescue aircraft to cover the Atlantic region, pointing out rightly that the area covered by air-sea rescue was far too vast to have to depend on aircraft stationed in Summerside or in Halifax. Yet to this date that recommendation has not been acted upon.
The judge also recommended that additional personnel be employed in the air-sea rescue centres to ensure maximum 24 hour efficiency. To the best of my knowledge that recommendation was not acted upon either. I think we deserve an explanation. People who depend upon the sea

April 14, 1976
Easter Adjournment
for a livelihood deserve an explanation. What is more important, we deserve from this government and from the Minister of Transport, who should have all the responsibility because he has under his command the Canadian coastguard, an assurance, while he is waiting for the report of this task force, that immediate steps will be taken to correct the inadequacies identified by the minister himself, and that they will put together some kind of interim organization to ensure maximum efficiency and capability and a reduction in reaction time until the report of the task force is received.
This would mean a few simple steps which I will suggest to the government right now. First of all, tracker aircraft should be stationed in Gander on a full time 24 hour basis. Second, lifeboats which were purchased by the government at considerable expense should be redesigned to make them efficient to the maximum, because at present they can only operate under ideal conditions. For example, when two fishermen were lost in Morton's Harbour in February there was a lifeboat standing by in Twillingate a short distance away and that lifeboat was not operational because it could not operate in more than two inches of ice.
One inch.

I am corrected by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Baker (Gander-Twillingate)), and I appreciate that correction.
Second, I am told that when the San Juan went down there was a lifeboat in St. John's at that time and that that lifeboat was not operational because it could not operate in high seas. These accidents do not take place under ideal conditions. They usually take place when there are high winds, adverse weather conditions or serious ice conditions, so for God's sake let us not play around with cosmetics. Let us bring these lifeboats back, redesign them, and have the necessary additions made to them which will make them truly operational.
Third, I suggest that some kind of plan be put into effect which would maximize the use of whatever aircraft and whatever vessels happen to be in the area. For example, at any given time at St. John's or Gander there are water bombers, which are converted Cansos, which are ideal for this type of operation and which could and should be brought into force whenever there is a rescue operation under way. This could be done by a simple arrangement with the government of Newfoundland. Surely that is a simple suggestion.
Finally, whatever the task force recommends-and obviously it will have to pay some heed to the recommendations of Judge Soper with respect to deployment-let us hope the government acts on its recommendations and acts with the dispatch this situation deserves.
In this regard I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment and Minister of Fisheries will let his voice be heard because I know he shares my concern. I know he is convinced, as I am, that the logical location for deployment of whatever facilities we have from Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island to cover the Newfoundland situation would be the airport at Gander, which has the National Defence establishment already

there. There is a fully operational aerodrome, and this could be done with very little additional expense to Canadian taxpayers. Whatever is to be done, for God's sake let it be done quickly, before someone else is lost.

speakeroldname: Mr. George Baker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment and Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), not in an effort to monopolize the debate on the adjournment motion, but simply to point out the truth which he speaks. This is a very important matter.
As the over-all arrangement for search and rescue is set up throughout this country we have four co-ordinating zones. In the case of the province the hon. member represents, which is my province, operations are co-ordinated from another province. All the aircraft which are used in search and rescue operations have to be sent from another province, and from a specific area of another province, which is perhaps quite distant.
The co-ordination presently in effect is not adequate at all. As the hon. member pointed out, division of authority between two specific departments is not acceptable. The triggering device for search and rescue is not acceptable, and I think that is the major reason why there are discussions under way regarding the whole situation.
What is it that the hon. member for St. John's East and I are basically requesting? We deserve at least an aircraft in our own province, which we do not have at present. We do not have one aircraft. They have to come from another area of Canada. The hon. member pointed out that with regard to the major disasters which have occurred that they have occurred mostly at a certain time of the year, and around the coast of Newfoundland. The hon. member pointed out the reasons for that.
We have fishermen who are licensed seal hunters and who have to go out at a time of year when the ice is in and not too far off shore. There is a regular hunting season, not for sports hunting, but to provide a food supplement to the people who live along our coast. They have to go out at a time of year when one normally would not be doing sports fishing. A sports fisherman would not want to be out among ice pans at a time of the year when any change in the weather within a 24-hour period would result in the sports fisherman being heavily iced in. Because of our geography, weather conditions, and the occupations of Newfoundlanders, I believe we deserve to have an air-sea rescue co-ordinating centre in Newfoundland.
I would not mind if the centre were placed in the riding of the hon. member, or in some other part of Newfoundland. However, Gander is a central location, and I think the government should reach that decision.
This question is important to Newfoundlanders, not just to those people working in the fishery who have to go out on these waters during the spring and winter months, but to everyone in Newfoundland. I predict that before long-I would say this summer-we will see some petitions about this matter presented in the House of Commons. I agree wholeheartedly with what the hon. member for St. John's East said with regard to the need for an air-sea rescue centre in Newfoundland and also with his general com-
April 14, 1976

ment about the need for co-ordination, better aircraft, and better equipment on that aircraft.
We could learn a lot if we examined some of the air-sea rescue services which are operated throughout the world. Perhaps if we were to look at what is now available, and deployed our resources properly, the problem would be solved. In any case, the problem has to be solved, and I join with the hon. member in making that point.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, it seems strange that after 17 months of a session, the longest in the history of this country, the adjournment motion should be put without any statement whatsoever from the government.
Nineteen months.

Well, I made a mistake in a conservative way. After that period of time the acting government House leader comes into the House and puts this motion for adjournment without any mention of any achievements the government could lay before the people of Canada as reasons for taking a recess instead of proroguing the House and starting a new session of parliament.
It is one of the very sad commentaries on this parliament that it has been going continuously since the last general election. That is an indication of just how unco-ordinated the government has been in everything it has tried to achieve, in the name of sanity, for the people of Canada. The crown the government wears is not a crown of diamonds and rubies. It is a crown of thorns, and the people of Canada feel the effects.
I am pleased to see the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) has been present in the House all the time this motion has been debated. He is new to the department. He is a dedicated man but must clean up a terrible mess in Atlantic Canada. Eight years ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) talked about the just society, about the need to eradicate regional economic disparity. Is it not sad that the head of the Economic Council of Canada, appearing before the Regional Development Committee, said that the department set up seven years ago to eliminate regional economic disparity has not achieved its aims? It has hardly lessened regional economic disparity which has existed since Confederation.
The economic outlook for people in my province becomes worse with each passing day. They face the future with fear and trepidation. Why, Mr. Speaker? The reason is our escalating energy costs. The blame is not to be laid so much at the feet of the federal government as at the feet of the government of Nova Scotia, which did virtually nothing by way of planning to lower the costs of energy. Our energy costs have escalated because the Nova Scotia government put its faith in offshore oil. Offshore oil is used mostly for the province's energy production. The situation is similar in Prince Edward Island but could have been avoided in Nova Scotia, as the province has available other resources
Easter Adjournment
which it could have brought on stream in anticipation of present difficulties.
Ordinary Nova Scotians owning ordinary homes pay more for their electric bills than for their mortgages. Mortgage payments are lower than payments for electric power bills. And this happened almost overnight. The government of Nova Scotia, through an advertising campaign, convinced people to change to electric heating. Many people converted, and now they cannot afford to heat their homes electrically. They cannot pay their electric bills and cannot sell their homes, because no one wants to buy homes so expensive to heat. This is a terrible mess and a terrible disaster for the people.
The federal government convinced many industries to locate in Nova Scotia. The idea was to provide employment for our people. Assisted by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, some industries established themselves in Nova Scotia. They face mounting energy costs which they could not have anticipated when they first moved to Nova Scotia. I do not doubt that if something is not done soon, bankruptcies in the province will increase. This will be bad news for the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the people of this country, because we shall lose the tremendous investment we made when we helped those industries locate in Nova Scotia.
I say to the minister that the Nova Soctia government's lack of planning and lack of concern for the people are reprehensible. I criticize the Department of Regional Economic Expansion for not protecting the investment the people of Canada made when they helped industries to locate in the province. My criticism is not directed at the minister personally; it is directed at departmental officials. They should have anticipated that energy costs would increase, and should have encouraged the government of Nova Scotia to provide forms of energy alternative to and cheaper than offshore oil.
Nova Scotia possesses tremendous coal resources and Devco, the federal entity, is doing its best to bring provincial coal on stream. It wants to open coal mines; we need coal both for the steel industry and thermal power production. When Devco was first established the government of Nova Scotia entered into a special arrangement with the federal government whereby Devco was to assume responsibility for the coal mines in Cape Breton and the Nova Scotia government for the coal mines in the rest of Nova Scotia. The provincial government was to pay the subventions connected with thermal power plants in the province, not the federal government. The Nova Scotia government thought it was a good deal. The federal government behaved generously in the deal which led to the establishment of the Crown corporation on Cape Breton Island. But what happened?
After the deal was signed and the Regan administration took over, the province began closing coal mines. It thought, shortsightedly, that it would save money because it would not need to pay subventions on coal if mines were closed. Now that administration would dearly love to have those coal mines in operation and dearly love to pay those subventions. In my constituency, at Springhill, a viable coal mine could be in operation. There is lots of coal. At one time the Nova Scotia government decided to open a

April 14, 1976
Easter Adjournment
new coal mine there, then, suddenly, at the whim of the premier, decided not to. In Pictou county it was the same.
The provincial government closed the mines. Because coal had no sex appeal for the premier, coal mining was phased out. He put all his eggs in the one basket. He put his faith in oil on Sable Island, until he discovered there wasn't much oil on Sable Island. There wasn't enough to make that oil commercially viable.
He showed everybody a bottle of oil.
Yes, he showed Nova Scotia a bottle of oil. Oil was to be the wave of the future in that part of Canada. But even that bottle of oil has become pretty expensive.
It has turned out to be castor oil.

As the hon. member from Kingston says, for Nova Scotia it has turned out to be castor oil.
Then the premier decided that, although we did not have offshore oil, perhaps we could develop Fundy tidal power. One minute he is in favour of Fundy tidal power, and the next he is not. Nobody knows where he stands. Despite the willingness of the federal government to involve itself in tidal power studies and bring closer the day when we can decide if we can harness the tides, the premier could not make up his mind. He could not come up with appointments to the Fundy tidal power review committee for almost a year. He messed around with the additional study and we lost months when the committee could have been working and coming up with conclusions. At this moment in time we in Nova Scotia find ourselves almost totally committed to offshore oil, and the premier now cries, asking the federal government to bail them out.
As much as I hate to see us having to pay for the mistakes of Mr. Regan in Nova Scotia, at the same time I say we have to give very serious consideration to meeting the request he is making. If not, we will only worsen the degree of regional economic disparity that exists there. We will increase unemployment in that area and there will be a further migration of our people because there will not be the possibilities to entice them to remain there. Therefore I say to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, please urge upon your colleagues to put into effect at least a short term program to help both Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island out of the terrible dilemma they are in with regard to escalating energy costs.
Let me give an example of how serious this is from a personal point of view, and I am much better able to pay my power bills than most people in my constituency. Prior to a few months ago my power bill was $24 for two months, in effect $12 a month. I have the same basic facilities now. I do not have an electric stove. I heat with oil, not with electricity. My water is oil heated. My power bill went from $24 to $83.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Did you talk to the provincial government?

The hon. member says I should talk to the provincial government. I agree with him from the point of view that it was the provincial government that created

the problem. However, the federal government has so much money invested in Nova Scotia through the infrastructure of DREE to try to overcome regional economic disparity that we cannot sacrifice what we have done, as well as the hundreds of millions of dollars of investment, because of the stupidity and incompetency of the Regan administration.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: It is the same in every province.

I hope it is not the same in every province. I suggest to the hon. member that everyone in this country does not have the same kind of power bill as the people in Nova Scotia. That is the sad fact. I therefore plead with the government to put forward some kind of interim plan to help the people of Nova Scotia get over the hump. The government should have some forward planning to open some coal mines, get on with the Fundy tidal power project, and get oil from wherever it can be found, but get away from the dependence on expensive offshore oil.
Even if we have to pay the equivalent for coal mined in Nova Scotia as we pay for offshore oil, it will accomplish two things. Nova Scotians will be put to work in the coal mines and pay cheques will be provided for them. Second, the money that we get for the coal that goes to the thermal power plants will stay in this country. Therefore, we must come up with some plan to try to overcome this tremendous economic burden that has quickly fallen on the shoulders of the people of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. We must try to keep the industries there viable. We must keep the people working in those industries and, hopefully, take some of the burden off the people of Nova Scotia who now are paying horrendous power rates. Many of the ordinary working people just cannot pay those rates as well as their mortgage payments. They will lose their homes.
This is a sad commentary on the shortsighted planning of the Regan administration in Nova Scotia that has now run crying to the federal government. At the same time, if we are going to protect our investment, we are forced to come up with some kind of interim plan that not only helps the people of Nova Scotia by eliminating regional economic disparity to a degree, but protects the investment the taxpayers of this country have made through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to overcome some of the unemployment that we face, and will continue to face in the days ahead.

Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to take only a few minutes of the time of the House to associate myself with the speeches which have been made by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and the hon. member for Gan-der-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) with regard to the need for immediate action in providing an effective search and rescue service on both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. I support completely the statements made by these two members with respect to conditions as they exist for fishermen on the Atlantic coast. I rise solely for the purpose of pointing out to the House that a similar situation exists on the Pacific coast and that the conditions there are equally deplorable and equally demand prompt and efficient action by the government.
April 14, 1976

On the Pacific coast last year, in a two week period during the herring fishing season, we lost 14 men and ten ships. Already this year, in the first two weeks of the season, we lost four men and six ships. When I raised the matter in the question period in the House some weeks ago, to our consternation the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) admitted that, while we have an aerial search capacity, we do not have an aerial rescue capacity after dark, and that for service during the night hours we are dependent upon the assistance of our good friends and neighbours in the United States.
During the storm which took the lives of those four men and was responsible for the sinking of those six ships, the United States Air Force was, of course, pre-occupied with events on its own coastline and we were unable to get the kind of service which might have saved the lives of the fishermen.
It becomes increasingly apparent that there are two great difficulties as far as the search and rescue arrangements on the Pacific Coast are concerned. The first is the lack of co-ordination. The Department of National Defence is involved, the Department of Transport is involved, the Department of Fisheries is involved and, in the case of night rescue operations, the U.S. Air Force is involved. It is no wonder the fishermen find the service unsatisfactory with a divided jurisdiction like that. They have complained to the government year after year, but no satisfactory action has followed.
Like the hon. member for St. John's East I was interested in the eight-page press release issued by the Department of Transport. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) seems to put the major blame for this loss of lives and ships upon the fishermen, not upon his department, not upon the government's inefficiency and incompetence, not on the fact that the operation is characterized by divided jurisdiction. I will read what the report says under the heading "Herring Roe Season":
Fishermen, in some cases, are not taking every precaution for their own safety. It is becoming evident, particularly during the herring roe season on the West Coast, that because of the cost involved fishermen are not willing to spend money to equip their boats with such safety equipment as emergency transmitter locators, flares and life jackets.
In 1975, 14 men died and 10 boats were lost in one two-week period. This year already, six boats have sunk and four men have lost their lives. However, there is nothing to prevent a novice crew from setting out under an incompetent captain on one of the many small, fragile gillnetters and running into trouble somewhere in the vast area served by the Victoria Rescue Co-ordinating Centre.
So the department is blaming the fishermen because they do not have proper equipment, because they have not taken precautions such as putting in bulkheads to prevent the fish moving and capsizing the boats. I would point out that the Department of Transport and the Department of Fisheries have been asked repeatedly by the unionized fishermen on the West Coast to make such provisions mandatory.
The fishermen have been asking the department for years to declare fish to be cargo under the fishing regulations; they have been asking the government to require that these fishermen shall instal on their boats necessary equipment such as transmitter locators, flares and life
Easter Adjournment
jackets. They have been asking that it be made mandatory for bulkheads to be put in and for the stern to be protected. Yet none of these requests have been complied with as yet.
Now, the minister, in the press release he issued, tells the country and the House that an inquiry has been undertaken. These are his words:
In July of last year, the report of the West Coast fishing vessel casualties inquiry was tabled in the House of Commons. It was initiated because of the unprecedented loss of life. The report made eight major recommendations on crew certification and training, weather forecasting, vessel regulations and inspection, fishing research, naval architecture and safety information to improve springtime operations.
I have this report in my hand. It is the West Coast Fishing Vessels Casualty Inquiry, March, 1975. It is a good report. But there is not a recommendation in it which has not been made to the government again and again over the years. The report of Mr. Justice Soper, to which the hon. member for St. John's East has referred, and the petitions and representations which have been made by the fishermen's union on the West Coast, have dealt again and again with these matters. Now the minister says he has received a report. And what does he propose to do with it? He says:
A joint Transport Canada-Fisheries working group has been studying the recommendations and how they should be implemented. The work of this group will result in meetings between senior Transport-Fisheries officials and all concerned parties, including the B.C. government, to discuss further the implementation of the recommendations. It has become evident that in spite of the provision of additional resources, facilities and co-ordination capabilities over the years, the marine SAR organisation is no longer entirely adequate.
A Canadian coastguard task force has reviewed the national search and rescue policy and the revised policy is expected to be ready for submission to cabinet by mid-1976.
They got the Soper Report in 1971. Briefs have repeatedly been presented to them by the fishermen's union. They have the report of the West Coast Fishing Vessels Casualty Inquiry in hand. And now the government says it hopes some recommendations will be ready for cabinet by midsummer of 1976. Then, of course, the House is perfectly aware that a decision made in Cabinet will not in itself do the fishermen any good because of the length of time it takes, after the time the cabinet has decided to do something, before the word trickles down through the bureaucracy and is translated into action. That interval, Mr. Speaker, is liable to be a lengthy one.
On Tuesday, April 8, I moved a motion in the House under Standing Order 43. It asked:
That the House urges the Prime Minister to order a restructuring of the search and rescue organization under a single agency responsible to one minister, and that immediate steps be taken to procure adequate facilities and equipment for air and marine search and rescue operations on a 24-hour basis.
Because it was put forward under Standing Order 43, requiring unanimous consent, the motion could not be dealt with-some Liberal members said no. I do not wish to delay the House but I do want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, and through you to the members of the government, that this is not a partisan matter; this is not some economic debate. It is a matter which affects the lives of the men who make a living by going out onto the ocean to catch fish. It is a matter which concerns the welfare of human beings, and the delay which the government has shown in coming to grips with this problem is deplorable.

April 14, 1976
Easter Adjournment
On almost every subject, but on this one in particular, members on the treasury benches opposite have shown themselves to be masters of procrastination. Their slogan seems to be: never do today what you can put off until tomorrow. The fishermen on the West Coast, like the fishermen on the East Coast, are sick and tired of this dilly-dallying. The government ought to take notice that members on both sides have stood up to register their righteous indignation and their protest.
We expect some action soon. By the time we come back after the recess we ought to hear from the Minister of Transport, if he is capable of coming down to earth, some information about what he and his colleagues propose to do to stop this deplorable loss of life due to the government's incompetence and to its failure to organize the search and rescue capability of our country under a single agency, and under one minister, so as to bring an end to this divided jurisdiction which has produced an intolerable situation.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 6(5)(a) I move:
That the sitting of the House be continued beyond the ordinary hour of daily sitting until this motion is adopted.

-which is met.

which the business under consideration should be interrupted-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I agree with what Your Honour has just said. I hope the hon. member will be recognized and will make a speech, and that other members who wish to make a speech will also do so. If the motion had not been agreed to we would have adjourned at six o'clock and sat tomorrow. As House leader I would only entreat members to make their points undoubtedly, but to endeavour to make them briefly.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether there is any broad agreement during this extended period, which I have no objection to, for the House to adopt a procedure whereby we will waive the quorum requirements during that period.

Before I get to the crux of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to explain why I put this motion. So often in this House individuals like myself who are on the backbenches do not have a proper opportunity to express the views and complaints of their constituents. We saw a prime example of this when the Liberal administration
April 14, 1976

brought in closure on the second reading debate of the gun control legislation.
Hear, hear!

If the hon. whip on the other side wishes to speak, he now has an opportunity. As I was saying, for the government's anti-inflation program to work it must have the faith of the public. This government, our Liberal administration, has lost the faith of the public because it speaks so often out of both sides of its mouth.
During the election of 1974 hon. members opposite said that our control program would not work. Now they themselves have introduced a program of selective controls for a period of three and a quarter years. This is a program with almost dictatorial powers that could lead to a state or government controlled economy. We advocated during the 1974 election campaign a 90 day freeze on everything, with a period of 18 months of flexible controls to follow.
What we wanted to do was to break the inflationary psychology that is prevalent in Canada, but we were also aware that controls were only a temporary stopgap program. However, the main plank in our program of controls was government restraint and the controlling of our money supply. This is not in the Liberal government's program.
The majority of economists today agree that the government itself bears the major responsibility for inflation because it has not controlled these two areas. What has the Liberal administration done in these two areas? It has asked the public to abide by an increase of 8 per cent while government expenditures rise to something in the vicinity of 18 per cent. I would ask our colleagues opposite, where is the fairness in that? Is it any wonder that the government has lost the faith of the Canadian public?
As I have said, in 1974 the Liberals campaigned against a controls policy. Then a year later they implement a program of controls which is full of injustices. I might also note that exactly the same thing happened in the 1972 election.
In 1972 the Conservative party proposed the indexing of personal income taxes and a modest increase for pensioners. We were criticized strongly by our opponents, but when they were elected as a minority government they accepted the guidelines upon which we campaigned. Now hon. members opposite wish to take credit for that. The other day in the House a Liberal backbencher was speaking and attempted to take credit for the conception and implementation of indexing of personal income tax, a positive platform of this party during the 1972 election campaign. We introduced that idea, and I commend the government for instituting programs we have introduced, but I think it could be a little more honest in presenting them to the people.
It is my feeling that the government cannot be trusted by the Canadian people, as illustrated by the examples I have given. In the last two elections the government has campaigned on one thing, and shortly after the election has reversed its position entirely.
There are other prime examples that leave a good many questions in the public's mind. All we have to do is look at
Easter Adjournment
the judges' affair, and there are many questions to be answered in that area, the SIU implications, the Hamilton Harbour scandal, the Sky Shops affair, the Mirabel airport inquiries, the Olympic Village and the travel agency irregularities. For any government to function properly it must have the faith of the public, but this Liberal administration does not have that faith, and understandably so.
Despite what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and other members of his government have said in the past about the danger of believing in "doom and gloom" forecasts, our economy remains in poor shape, and we believe it is due to the contradictory economic policies of the present administration-
An. hon. Member: Why don't you read?

April 14, 1976
Easter Adjournment
We have the potential to be the wealthiest people on earth if we allow our resources to be harnessed through individual initiative.
He also said that:
-left to government, our oil fields, our gas reserves and our potash industry would never have been developed to their present levels. Yet governments, in the name of progress, now stifle further advances through heavy taxation and regulation.
He told the House of Commons:
The nation has now reached a crossroads where we must decide between a more competitive more open society or accept, perhaps irrevocably, a society in which the large decisions about our economic and personal welfare are made by a central government.
This same government would like to run all our lives, but it should be remembered just how it runs its own departments such as the Post Office. The hon. member for York-Simcoe went on to state:
The past demonstrates that a system of free enterprise, despite its many flaws, is the most compatible with the protection of rights and liberties as well as the most productive of material goods.
There are two other areas I wish to deal with, and one is in respect of Bill C-83. I should like to express my deep concern and disappointment with the Liberal administration that has seen fit to muzzle members on all sides of this House on the second reading debate of Bill C-83. All this does is exemplify the attitude of the government. It does not care about what the people want. It is going to do exactly what it wants, and it does not give the members of this House the opportunity to express the wishes and the desires of the constituents they are sent here to serve.
Hear, hear!

In closing I should like to give a prime example of what is happening in my own constituency of Pembina. The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) said to me several months back that in the event our constituents and the people in the municipal district of Sturgeon did not wish to have a federal penitentiary located in the area, the government would not go ahead with it. What do we see happening now? The Solicitor General is pushing this down the throats of the individuals in this area, in spite of the fact there is a petition on his desk with the signatures of 248 people requesting that the government not build this penitentiary on this piece of prime agricultural land.
Shame!

I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is this not being less than honest with the Canadian people regarding this issue?
In concluding, I should like to leave you on a lighter note, Mr. Speaker. I wish you, the members of the House, and the staff, all a restful and happy Easter.
Mr. Speaker, I am aware of the desire of many members to leave the Chamber and I will not impose upon you for very long.
Hear, hear!

That may be the only response I get.
It probably is appropriate that one of the last speakers this afternoon intends to talk about the environment, because the environment is the last thing on the priority

list not only of the government, not only in terms of the opposition, but in terms of the public itself.
What about the NDP?

Yes, and the NDP. I am not trying to be partisan. What I am trying to do is bring the question back to the attention of the public.
As soon as the gross national product in this country drops a little bit, interest in the environment drops as well. We are all guilty in this regard. The environment was something we talked about several years ago and something the government talked about in the Speech from the Throne in 1974. This is what the government said in that famous speech about its intentions:
-stemming the despoilation of our planet and returning our water, air and land to a more natural state.
That is a very acceptable objective, but nothing has been done about it. Not only is the government not attempting to redress this process of the environment, it is participating in the escalation of the destruction of this country's environment at a rate that is disgraceful.
Let us have a look at what the government has been doing. The last thing it did was to replace the minister we had before. She was not particularly successful at her job but she could have learned, with a little time and patience. She made some very attractive speeches. Her rhetoric was very good, as were her intentions. What did the government do? It moved her out as soon as it looked like she might really start to do something in respect of the environment.
The government replaced that minister with the most moveable minister in the whole Liberal cabinet. He began his career without a portfolio. Then he went to DREE. We remember when that minister was looking after DREE. I would say that we in the New Democratic Party were thankful that he was responsible for DREE in 1972, because he was probably as responsible as any other minister for the election of many members of our party due to the way he managed that portfolio. Then he went to the Department of Transport. We remember that. After he looked around that department he said it was in a mess and that he could not do anything about it. Then the government tried to find another slot for him. I forgot for a moment that he was once in the Department of Manpower and Immigration. Finally he went to the Department of the Environment. That minister has a reverse Midas touch. Everything he touches becomes crap.
I should like to say something about the important decision the government will make tomorrow in respect of the Beaufort Sea. My prediction is that this drilling permit will be issued. The reason is that the same mistake has been made that was made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) in respect of the Lockheed Orion. Two years ago an agreement was entered into in principle with Dome Petroleum Company involving an investment of $100 million. The government locked itself into that project. Then the government received the environment studies which predict the probable disaster and high risk in terms of the use of the Beaufort Sea area. Now it is faced with either a $100 million lawsuit, or risk to the
April 14, 1976

environment. I predict the government will let the environment take the risk again despite the protest by the United States. There again the government has locked itself into a position out of sheer negligence.
Then there is the Syncrude project in which there is a conflict of interest. The environmental studies refer to 40 tons, and the emission permit is for 287 long tons. In this country we rely for our standard of living on the industrialization of the belt immediately north of us. When our standard of living results in the death of Indians from mercury poisoning the government should take another look at the environment in terms of things we should be examining in this House. Last but not least in respect of the environment is the insatiable desire we have for money. We export nuclear death around the world. The government is contributing to the greatest possible disaster the world has yet seen.
Hogwash.

It is not hogwash. We were once known around the world as a country on which one could count to go abroad and cool the fires of international tension. Now we are flooding the world with CANDU reactors. It is interesting that the United States, in terms of their sales of the Westinghouse reactor, say there is no point in bothering with unstable countries because Canada has them all locked up.
The United States takes the position that there is no point in considering sales to North Korea or Argentina because the Canadians are selling their reactors to these countries at an indecent rate. Then there is the question of our reliance on domestic nuclear sales. There is required in this country a very open inquiry so that the public will have an important input. We may be creating a nuclear industry which will be completely unnecessary if we look to alternate sources of power. If we continue to do what we are doing we will rue the day.
I must say that for the first time I am ashamed of Canada's position in the world in terms of the export of nuclear reactors. I might say that the government is a very poor inheritor of the mantle of Lester B. Pearson who went down in history as a peace maker. This country may go down in history as a war maker and a contributor to international disaster.
Easter Adjournment

I am happy, on behalf of the Speaker and at his express request, to invite all hon. members as well as staff members, and members of the press, to come and fraternize in Room 16, and perhaps discuss all the topics mentioned in the last few minutes, in the spirit of Easter and the Resurrection.
